text: Now Adam knew his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. She said, "I have gained a man with the LORD's help."

versions.text: Adam knew his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. She said, "I have brought forth a man with the LORD's help."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb qaniti ("I have acquired/gained") forms a deliberate sound-play with the name Qayin (Cain); "brought forth" obscures that link and also duplicates the sense of "gave birth" in the previous clause. "Gained" (or "gotten") preserves the acquisition sense and the echo of the name while remaining smooth for reading aloud. Adding the opening "Now" reflects the introductory waw and eases the transition into the new narrative section.

footnotes.text: The final clause is one of the most disputed in the Hebrew Bible. Literally it reads "I have gotten/acquired a man ’et-YHWH." The particle ’et normally marks a direct object, which would yield the startling "I have gotten a man, namely the LORD"; but ’et can also function as the preposition "with," giving "with the LORD" — that is, with his help or in partnership with him. The translation follows the second option and supplies the word "help," which is not in the Hebrew but makes the sense clear when read aloud. Other defensible renderings are "I have gotten a man with the LORD," "I have produced a man like the LORD," or "from the LORD." The verb "knew" is retained rather than a modern equivalent because it preserves the dignity and reticence of the Hebrew idiom for marital intimacy, and "Now" at the opening signals the shift from the garden narrative to a new episode.

The verb yada‘, "to know," is the standard Hebrew idiom for sexual union, implying personal knowledge rather than mere physical act. Eve's exclamation turns on a play of sound: qaniti ("I have gotten/acquired/created") echoes the name Qayin (Cain). It is an assonantal wordplay rather than a strict etymology; the name Cain most likely derives from a root meaning "smith" or "metalworker" (compare the noun qayin, "spear"). The verb qanah itself carries a range from "buy, acquire" to "create, bring forth," as when God is called "maker of heaven and earth." Eve says ’ish, "a man," not "a son" or "a boy" — an unusual and emphatic word choice.

Eve's words are the first human speech after the expulsion from the garden, and they sound a note of hope: life continues, and she credits the LORD as partner in bringing it forth. Some interpreters have heard in "I have gotten a man, the LORD" an early messianic expectation, as though Eve believed the promised offspring who would crush the serpent had already arrived; on this reading the narrative immediately deflates her hope, since Cain becomes the first murderer. Others hear pride or presumption — a woman claiming creative power alongside God. Most read it simply as grateful acknowledgment that children come as a gift from God, a theme repeated throughout Scripture.

The ancient versions already struggled with the phrase and generally avoided identifying the child with God: the Greek tradition renders it "through God," the old Aramaic paraphrase "from before the LORD," and the Latin "through God." These readings likely reflect interpretation of a difficult text rather than a different Hebrew wording; the consonantal text is stable in the manuscript tradition.

In the ancient Near East, bearing a child — especially a son — secured a family's future, its labor force, and its claim to land. Naming was ordinarily the mother's prerogative in these narratives, and the name given often commemorated the circumstances of birth or the mother's words at the moment. Cain and Abel represent the two basic modes of subsistence in the region, settled farming and pastoral herding, whose tensions are reflected in the story that follows.

text: Later she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel became a keeper of sheep, and Cain worked the ground.

versions.text: Later she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel became a keeper of sheep, and Cain worked the soil.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'adamah' occurs here ('oved adamah') and again in the next verse, where it is rendered 'ground' ('fruit of the ground'). Rendering it consistently as 'ground' preserves the deliberate wordplay with 'Adam' and helps a listener hear the link between Cain's occupation and his offering. 'Worked the ground' also reads with the same natural rhythm as 'worked the soil.'

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally reads "and she added to bear his brother Abel" — the verb yasaf ("to add, do again") is a common idiom for repeating an action. Rendering it "Later she gave birth" keeps the natural forward motion of spoken narrative; alternatives are "Again she gave birth" or "She bore another son." Note that no separate word for conceiving appears here, unlike verse 1. The second half of the verse uses two matching participial descriptions: Abel "was a shepherd of flock" and Cain "was a worker of ground." "Keeper of sheep" preserves the older phrasing that reads well aloud, while "worked the ground" avoids the clumsier "tiller of the soil." The Hebrew tso'n covers small livestock generally, sheep and goats together, so "flocks" is equally defensible.

Abel's name in Hebrew is Hevel, the same word that means "breath, vapor, mist" — the word repeated dozens of times in Ecclesiastes for what is fleeting and insubstantial. Unlike Cain, whose name the previous verse ties to Eve's exclamation (qaniti, "I have gained"), Abel's name is given without explanation, which many readers have felt is itself part of the storytelling. Cain's occupation, oved adamah ("one who serves/works the ground"), uses the same verb-and-noun pair found in the garden account, where the man was placed to work the ground he was taken from; the phrase quietly links Cain back to Adam's task.

The verse presents the two brothers' occupations side by side without ranking them. Both shepherding and farming are portrayed elsewhere in Scripture as honorable callings, so the story that follows is not a contest between ways of life; the difference lies in the brothers themselves, not their trades. Readers who hear "vapor" in Abel's name have long taken it as a foreshadowing of how brief his life will be. The order of birth also matters: as in later narratives, the younger son becomes the one whose offering is received.

Mixed livelihoods of this kind were normal in the ancient Near East: settled households grew grain and other crops while family members pastured sheep and goats on land unsuited to cultivation. The two brothers therefore represent complementary halves of a single village economy rather than rival cultures. Each will bring the natural yield of his own labor as a gift — grain and produce from the field, an animal from the flock.

The Hebrew tradition here is stable, and the ancient translations follow it closely. Some early retellings outside the biblical text supply additional details the verse omits — names for the brothers' sisters, or the claim that the two boys were twins, an inference drawn from the absence of a second mention of conceiving in this verse. These are interpretive expansions rather than manuscript evidence.

text: In the course of time Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground as an offering to the LORD,

versions.text: In time Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground,
versions.explanation: Two small gains: (1) 'In the course of time' renders מִקֵּץ יָמִים ('at the end of days') a bit more fully than the clipped 'In time' while still reading smoothly aloud; (2) restoring the Hebrew order — object first, then the designation 'as an offering to the LORD' — avoids the slight ambiguity of 'brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground,' where 'from the fruit' can momentarily attach to 'the LORD.' The partitive מִן is kept with 'some of.' The comma linking to verse 4 is retained.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with an idiom, literally "and it came to be at the end of days." Since "days" here marks an unspecified stretch of time rather than a fixed number, the rendering "In the course of time" keeps the vagueness of the original. Other defensible renderings include "after some time," "in due season," or (taking "days" as a year, as it can mean elsewhere) "at the end of the year" or "at harvest time." The partitive "some of the fruit" reflects the Hebrew preposition min, which marks a portion taken from a larger whole; the same construction reappears in the next verse with Abel's flock. "Offering" translates minchah, a general word for a gift or tribute; "gift," "tribute," or "present" would also fit. The verse ends with a comma because verses 3 and 4 form a single balanced sentence in Hebrew, and reading them as one flowing unit preserves the pairing of the two brothers. "The LORD" stands for the divine name YHWH, following the long-standing convention of representing it with a title in capitals.

The phrase miqqets yamim combines qets, "end, limit," with yamim, "days." Hebrew often uses "days" loosely for a season or even a full year, so the expression resists precise dating. There is a quiet play on words running through the passage: Cain is the one who works the adamah (ground), and it is from the fruit of the adamah that he brings his gift — the very ground that will later swallow his brother's blood and turn against him. The verb heviʾ ("brought") is repeated in verse 4, setting the two brothers side by side in identical grammatical dress.

This is the first act of worship recorded in Scripture, and it happens without any command, altar, or priest being mentioned — the impulse to bring a gift to God appears simply as something human beings do. Interpreters have long debated why Cain's offering was not accepted. Some point to the wording itself: Abel brings firstborn animals and the choice fat portions, while Cain brings merely "some of the fruit," with no note of quality or first yield. Others argue the difference lay not in the substance but in the heart, since the text says the LORD looked with favor on "Abel and his offering" — the person before the gift. Later reflection in the New Testament attributes Abel's acceptance to faith. A further reading holds that grain offerings are elsewhere fully acceptable, so the narrative deliberately withholds an explanation, leaving God's freedom unexplained.

The two brothers represent the two basic modes of subsistence in the ancient Near East: settled farming and pastoral herding. Bringing the first or best produce of field and flock to a deity was common practice across the region, understood as tribute acknowledging the divine owner of the land and its fertility. The word minchah was also used in ordinary life for the tribute a subject brought to a king, which colors the scene: the brothers approach God as one approaches a sovereign. Israel's later law would formalize such gifts as offerings of firstfruits and firstborn, but here the practice appears in its earliest, unregulated form.

text: and Abel too brought an offering, some of the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions. The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering,

versions.text: and Abel brought an offering too, from the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions. The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering,
versions.explanation: The Hebrew emphatic "gam-hu" attaches to Abel himself, so placing "too" right after "Abel" better reflects the emphasis and reads more smoothly aloud than the trailing "an offering too." Also, "some of the firstborn" mirrors the partitive "mi-" used for Cain's offering in the previous verse, keeping the parallel structure clear for a listener.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "And Abel brought, he too, from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat." The emphatic "he too" (gam-hu') has been rendered "Abel too" and placed early for smoother speech, and the word "offering" — implied by the parallel with verse 3 and by "his offering" later in this verse — is supplied so the sentence stands on its own when read aloud. The Hebrew "from" (min) before both nouns signals a portion taken from a larger whole, hence "some of the firstborn." The final phrase could also be rendered "their fat ones," that is, the fattest of the flock, rather than "their fat portions"; the wording chosen keeps the sacrificial overtone that the ancient versions heard here. "Looked with favor on" renders a verb that means simply "to gaze at, regard"; "had regard for," "accepted," or "paid attention to" are all possible, but the choice here allows the same phrase to carry over into verse 5 in the negative.

The verb sha'ah means to look at, gaze upon, or turn one's attention toward, and with the preposition 'el it conveys regard bordering on approval. Nothing in the verb itself describes fire, smoke, or any visible sign; the text says only that the LORD looked. The word for "fat," chelev, denotes the rich suet of an animal and, by extension, the choicest part of anything. The feminine plural suffix in "their fat" agrees grammatically with the individual animals of the flock (tso'n is a collective noun). Note also the tight sound-play running through the passage: Hebrel (Abel) hevi' (brought) — the names and verbs of these brothers are woven together in Hebrew.

Two details distinguish Abel's gift from Cain's: it is drawn from the firstborn and from the fat, both terms later marking what belongs to God by right and what is best. In Israel's law the firstborn of the flock and the fat of a sacrifice were reserved for the LORD. Shepherding and farming were the two basic livelihoods of the ancient Near East, and both grain and animal offerings were normal; the narrative is not pitting one occupation or one kind of sacrifice against the other.

The text conspicuously withholds any explanation for why the LORD regarded Abel's offering. Interpreters have proposed several answers: that Abel gave the best while Cain gave merely "some of the fruit"; that the LORD's freedom in choosing cannot be reduced to a formula; that the difference lay in the worshipers' hearts rather than in the gifts, an approach taken up in the New Testament, where Abel's sacrifice is credited to faith. Later Jewish and Christian tradition also read the shepherd's blood offering as pointing forward to atonement. The restraint of the Hebrew narrative should caution against pressing any single explanation too far.

text: but on Cain and his offering he did not look with favor. Cain burned with fierce anger, and his face fell.

versions.text: but on Cain and his offering he did not look with favor. Cain burned with anger, and his face fell.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew intensifier מְאֹד ("very, exceedingly") in וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד is not represented. "Burned with fierce anger" conveys the intensity while keeping the verse's oral rhythm and preserving the burn/fall imagery echoed in verse 6.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew places the rejected party first — "and to Cain and to his offering he did not look" — mirroring in reverse the word order of verse 4, where the LORD's favorable look comes first and Abel second. The rendering "but on Cain and his offering he did not look with favor" keeps that fronted emphasis while opening with "but" so the contrast is audible when read aloud. The verb translated "look with favor" (sha'ah) is the same verb used of Abel in the previous verse; repeating the full English phrase preserves the deliberate echo rather than varying the wording for style. "Cain burned with fierce anger" unpacks a compact Hebrew idiom that literally says only "it burned to Cain greatly"; alternatives include "Cain became very angry" or "Cain was greatly incensed." The final clause is kept concrete — "his face fell" — rather than smoothed into "he scowled" or "he was downcast," because the next verse quotes God using the very same image.

The verb sha'ah means to gaze at or regard attentively, and by extension to look upon with acceptance; it is a verb of attention, not of eating or consuming, so nothing is said here about fire or visible signs. The anger idiom uses charah, "to burn, be hot," in an impersonal construction with the preposition le- ("it burned to Cain"); the noun for anger, 'aph — which also means "nose" or "nostril" — is often supplied but is absent here, leaving the heat itself as the subject. Hebrew thus pictures rage as internal combustion. The plural verb with "his face" (panim is grammatically plural) yields "his faces fell," an idiom for a countenance sinking in resentment or dejection. There is also a sound play running through the passage between charah (burn with anger) and the later warning about mastering sin, and between the falling of Cain's face here and God's question in the next verse, which repeats the identical verb.

The text gives no explicit reason for the rejection, and interpreters have long filled the silence. Some point to the details of verse 4 — Abel brought firstborn animals and the choicest fat portions, while Cain's gift is described simply as fruit of the ground — and infer a difference in care or generosity. Others locate the difference in the giver rather than the gift, reading the episode as a matter of faith and inner disposition, a line taken up in later scriptural reflection. Still others stress divine freedom in election, noting that Scripture repeatedly favors the unexpected or the younger. What the narrative does emphasize is what happens next: God does not abandon Cain but addresses him directly with questions, treating the burning anger as a moment still open to choice. The falling face marks the first appearance of murderous resentment in the human story, and the placement of anger immediately after worship is itself a theological statement about how quickly devotion can curdle into rivalry.

In the ancient Near East the face was the primary register of a person's standing and inner state; to have one's face "lifted" signified acceptance and honor, while a fallen or lowered face signaled shame, grief, or smoldering resentment. The pairing of an offering with a divine gaze reflects a wider cultural assumption that a gift's acceptance had to be signaled somehow, though this narrative deliberately withholds any description of how Cain knew. Sacrificial practice in the region regularly reserved the fat and the firstborn as the portions of highest value, which is why the earlier verse specifies them.

The ancient Greek tradition renders the anger clause differently, saying that the matter grieved Cain greatly, and describes his face as collapsing or falling in — a reading that emphasizes sorrow more than rage. The Hebrew consonantal text is stable here, and the Greek is best explained as an interpretive softening or an attempt to render the burning idiom into idiomatic Greek. The later question in verse 6, which presupposes anger, supports the Hebrew reading.

text: Then the LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry? Why has your face fallen?

versions.text: The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry? Why has your face fallen?
versions.explanation: Adding "Then" reflects the narrative sequence of the Hebrew verb form and gives smoother oral flow after the preceding verse, which ends with Cain's fallen face. The rest of the rendering is accurate; the open quotation correctly carries into the next verse.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "Why is it hot to you, and why have your face fallen?" — the same two idioms used in verse 5 to describe Cain's reaction ("burned" and "his face fell"). The translation deliberately echoes verse 5's wording so that the reader hears the LORD quoting Cain's own condition back to him. "Why are you angry?" renders the idiom in natural English rather than the wooden "why has it burned to you"; the more literal "why are you so incensed" was considered but judged too heavy for reading aloud. "Why has your face fallen?" is kept close to the Hebrew because the image is vivid and comprehensible, and because it preserves the pairing with the previous verse; alternatives such as "why do you look so downcast" or "why is your face downcast" smooth the idiom away. Note also that the questions are genuine questions, not accusations — the punctuation and phrasing keep them open, inviting a response.

The verb חָרָה (charah) means "to burn, be kindled," used impersonally with the preposition לְ: "it burned to/for Cain." The full idiom often includes אַף ("nose, nostril"), i.e. "his nose burned" — anger pictured as flaring nostrils and heat rising in the body. Here אַף is omitted, leaving the bare impersonal construction. The second idiom, נָפְלוּ פָנֶיךָ ("your face has fallen"), describes a downcast, sullen expression; its opposite is the "lifted face" (נָשָׂא פָנִים), which appears in the next verse in the word שְׂאֵת ("lifting up"). The double לָמָּה ("why... why...") is an emphatic rhetorical pairing typical of Hebrew poetry and heightened speech.

God addresses Cain directly and questioningly before any act of violence, just as he questioned Adam and Eve in the garden. The pattern is consistent: the divine interrogation is not information-gathering but an invitation to self-examination and turning back. Many readers see here a statement about divine mercy preceding judgment — Cain is warned before he sins, and again after (v. 9). The questions also imply that Cain's anger, though real, is answerable: it is a state he can be called out of rather than a fate. This underlies the moral appeal of verse 7, where mastery over sin is presented as possible.

In the ancient Near East, the face was the primary index of a person's inner state and social standing. A "fallen face" signaled shame, resentment, or loss of honor, while a "raised face" signaled acceptance and favor. God's non-acceptance of Cain's offering is therefore experienced not merely as private disappointment but as public dishonor — a loss of face in the fullest sense — which helps explain the intensity of his reaction and the violence that follows.

text: If you do what is right, will you not be lifted up? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at the door. It desires to have you, but you must master it."

footnotes.text: The verse is among the most difficult in the book, and the translation aims for a readable rendering that preserves its ambiguity rather than resolving it. "Do what is right" renders a single Hebrew verb meaning "to do well, to do good, to make good"; it may refer to right conduct generally or, more narrowly, to bringing a proper offering. "Will you not be lifted up?" renders a bare Hebrew noun-form meaning "lifting, raising"; since the previous verse speaks of Cain's face having "fallen," the phrase most naturally answers it as a lifting of the face, that is, restored acceptance and dignity — and the rendering deliberately echoes that image. Other readings are possible and long-established: "there is forgiveness" (since the same idiom can mean to bear or take away guilt), or "you will be accepted." "Crouching" renders a participle used of animals lying in wait. "It desires to have you" makes explicit the force of a Hebrew phrase that says only "its desire is toward you." "You must master it" renders a verb form that can be read as a promise ("you will rule over it"), a command, or a possibility ("you can rule over it"); the modal "must" preserves the note of summons that the context of divine warning suggests.

The Hebrew here is famously terse and grammatically uneven. The word for "sin" (chattat) is feminine, but the participle "crouching" is masculine, and the following pronoun "its desire" is likewise masculine — one reason many readers hear the clause as personifying sin as a lurking creature rather than describing an abstract quality. The word chattat itself does double duty in the Hebrew Bible, meaning both "sin" and "sin offering," and some have heard both senses at the door. The verb translated "crouching" (rovets) is used of animals lying down, especially of a beast at rest or in ambush. The final clause, "its desire is toward you, but you shall rule over it," repeats almost word for word the phrasing spoken to the woman in 3:16, a deliberate verbal echo that binds the two scenes of temptation and consequence together.

The Akkadian word rābiṣu, cognate with the Hebrew participle for "crouching," designates a demon that lies in wait at doorways and thresholds in Mesopotamian texts. Ancient Near Eastern households treated the threshold as a vulnerable boundary, guarded with rituals and protective figures. If that background is in play, the image is of a threshold demon poised to spring — a picture Cain's contemporaries would have found vivid and immediate.

The verse presents the pivotal moment of moral freedom in the story: Cain is warned before he acts, and told that mastery over the crouching power is within reach. The wording has carried enormous weight in discussions of human free will and the inclination toward evil; some traditions read the closing clause as a firm promise that sin need not prevail, others as a command that Cain tragically refuses. The echo of 3:16 also raises the question of how the desire-and-rule language functions: here it plainly describes something to be resisted and overcome, which has shaped how many read the earlier verse as well. The Lord's speech shows judgment preceded by warning — grace offered before the deed, not only after it.

The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult enough that the ancient versions diverge widely. The early Greek translation reads something quite different: "if you offer correctly but do not divide correctly, have you not sinned? Be still," apparently reflecting either a different reading tradition or an attempt to make sense of a hard text. The Aramaic paraphrases expand it into extended moral commentary about repentance, judgment, and the evil inclination. The Hebrew tradition preserved by the Masoretes is consistent across manuscripts, and the translation follows it; the variety in the versions reflects the difficulty of the wording rather than genuine competing texts.

text: Cain spoke to his brother Abel. And while they were out in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew says literally "And Cain said to his brother Abel" — but no words of speech follow. Since the Hebrew verb "said" with the preposition "to" normally introduces direct quotation, the rendering here uses "spoke to," which lets the sentence stand as a complete statement without inventing words Cain never speaks in the received Hebrew text. Other possible renderings are "Cain told his brother Abel [what the LORD had said]" or, following several ancient versions, "Cain said to his brother Abel, 'Let us go out to the field.'" The abrupt silence is preserved deliberately: the reader hears the opening of a conversation and then only the violence. In the second half, "rose up against" translates a Hebrew phrase that literally reads "arose to his brother Abel"; the sense of hostile assault is clear from what follows.

The name Abel (Hebrew Hevel) is the same word used for "vapor, breath, fleeting nothingness" — the word that dominates Ecclesiastes. The name quietly anticipates how brief his life will be. The verb translated "killed" (harag) denotes deliberate slaying rather than accidental death; it is not the technical term of the later legal codes but a blunt word for taking life. Note also the insistent repetition of "his brother" — three times in two verses — which the Hebrew uses to press home that this is fratricide, not merely homicide. The preposition after "rose up" is the ordinary "to" rather than the expected "against," a slightly unusual construction that some read as "rose up toward," as if Cain got up and went over to him.

The Masoretic text has an unusual break marked in the middle of this verse, right after "his brother," which ancient scribes evidently understood as a gap where speech once stood or should stand. The Samaritan Hebrew tradition, the early Greek translation, the Syriac, and the Latin all supply the words "Let us go out to the field," which fits the following clause about their being in the field. It is debated whether these versions preserve an older reading lost from the Hebrew or whether they smooth over a difficulty by filling the silence. The traditional Hebrew text is followed here.

The "field" is the open country beyond settlement and cultivation — a place without witnesses. The narrative reflects an agrarian world in which the shepherd and the tiller share the same land but not the same livelihood, and where blood-vengeance for a slain kinsman was the ordinary expectation. That expectation makes the following scene, where God himself takes up Abel's cause, all the more striking.

Immediately after the warning of verse 7 — "you must master it" — Cain does the opposite: sin crouching at the door is admitted rather than ruled. The first death in Scripture is thus a murder, and it happens within a family and in the aftermath of worship. Later writers make Abel the first of the righteous martyrs whose blood cries out, and they read Cain's act as the fruit of hatred rather than a sudden loss of control. The silence where Cain's words should be has often been heard as the silence of premeditation: what he said to his brother was not worth recording, because it was only a lure.

text: Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?" He answered, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?"

footnotes.text: The divine name here is the four-letter Hebrew name YHWH, represented by "the LORD" in capitals, following long-standing convention that reflects the Jewish practice of reading "Adonai" (my Lord) in its place. "Then the LORD said" renders the ordinary Hebrew narrative chain (literally "and the LORD said"); "Then" carries the sequence forward from the murder in the previous verse without adding weight. The second speech is introduced in Hebrew by the same plain verb, "and he said"; it is rendered "He answered" because English dialogue reads more naturally when a reply is marked as a reply, and the oral rhythm benefits from the variation. The word order of Cain's retort in Hebrew is emphatic — roughly "The keeper of my brother — am I?" — with the pronoun standing last for stress; English cannot easily reproduce this without sounding stilted, so the familiar and rhythmically strong "Am I my brother's keeper?" is retained. Alternatives such as "my brother's guardian" or "the one who watches over my brother" are defensible but lose the terse, insolent snap of the Hebrew.

The question uses the short interrogative particle 'ey, "where?", a clipped form beside the fuller 'ayyeh. It echoes God's earlier question to Adam, "Where are you?" — the same pattern of a searching question that opens a way back rather than gathering information. The word rendered "keeper" is the participle shomer, from the root sh-m-r, "to guard, watch, keep, tend." The same root describes the human task of "keeping" the garden and later the LORD's own keeping of his people. There is bitter irony in the vocabulary: Abel was a shepherd, one who watches over the flock, and Cain now sneers at the idea that anyone should have to watch over the watchman. The threefold repetition of "brother" in the surrounding verses — Cain's brother, your brother, my brother — hammers the relationship that Cain is trying to shrug off, and his final word, the emphatic pronoun 'anokhi ("I"), leaves him standing alone in his own sentence.

In Israelite legal custom a shomer was a recognized role: a person entrusted with another's property — livestock, goods, a deposit — and answerable for its loss. Cain's reply may therefore carry a legal edge: "Have I been contracted to guard him?" He answers a question about kinship with the language of property law, as though obligation existed only where a formal arrangement had been made. The scene itself takes the shape of a trial: interrogation, denial, evidence (the blood), verdict, sentence, and finally a protective mark.

Cain's "I do not know" is the first outright lie spoken to God in the biblical narrative, and it marks a deepening from his parents' evasions, who hid and shifted blame but did not deny. The rhetorical question that follows is one of Scripture's great self-condemnations: the answer that the rest of the Bible gives is yes — we are indeed responsible for one another. God's question, like "Where are you?" in the garden, is not an inquiry but a summons to confession; that Cain refuses it shapes everything that follows. Readers have long taken this verse as the foundation of the biblical ethic of neighbour-love and of communal responsibility for the vulnerable, and it stands behind later teaching that hatred of a brother is itself a form of murder. Note also that God does not abandon Cain despite the refusal; judgment comes, but so does protection.

Unlike the previous verse, where the ancient versions supply words of Cain that the traditional Hebrew text lacks, this verse is transmitted with essential uniformity across the Hebrew manuscripts and the early translations. The ancient Greek and Syriac versions and the Aramaic paraphrases all render it substantially as it stands here, though the Aramaic paraphrases expand Cain's reply into a longer speech disputing divine justice — an interpretive elaboration rather than a variant reading.

text: The LORD said, "What have you done? Listen—your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground!

versions.text: The LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground.
versions.explanation: "The voice of your brother's blood" is a stilted mouthful for oral reading. Hebrew qol here functions as an attention-getter, so rendering it as "Listen—" preserves the force of the idiom while giving the line a cleaner spoken rhythm; the blood then becomes the natural subject of the verb. The quotation is left open since the divine speech continues into the next verse.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew simply reads "And he said"; the subject is carried over from verse 9. Because verse 9 contains speech by both the LORD and Cain, the speaker is named here ("The LORD said") so that a listener following by ear knows at once whose voice this is. The Hebrew opens the accusation with the noun qol, "voice" or "sound," which many renderings keep as "the voice of your brother's blood is crying out." Hebrew, however, often uses qol as an attention-getting interjection — something like "Hark!" or "Listen!" — and that is how it is taken here, giving a short, urgent beat before the accusation lands, which reads better aloud than the heavier construct chain. The plural Hebrew noun "bloods" is rendered by the English collective "blood," since English does not pluralize the word this way; the plural verb of the Hebrew is likewise smoothed to "is crying out." The closing exclamation mark reflects the force of the divine outcry, and the quotation is left open because the speech continues without a break into verse 11.

Two features of the Hebrew are worth noting. First, demei ("bloods," plural) is the regular idiom for blood violently shed — bloodguilt — rather than blood in the veins; the plural intensifies rather than counts. Second, the verb tsa'aq describes the shriek of a victim of injustice: it is the cry of the oppressed Israelites in Egypt and the legal outcry of one who has been wronged and appeals for redress. So the image is not a ghostly whisper but a formal appeal for justice lodged with the highest court. The word for "ground," adamah, is the same word from which the man (adam) was formed and which he was to till; it recurs in the next verse, where the ground itself "opens its mouth," binding the two verses together by keyword. God's question "What have you done?" echoes the interrogation in the garden and is a summons to account rather than a request for information.

The verse establishes a principle that runs through the rest of Scripture: innocent blood is never simply lost, but calls out for justice and defiles the land on which it is spilled, so that the land must be cleansed. God is presented as the one who hears the cry of the victim even when no human witness exists — Abel has no advocate, no burial, no legal standing, and yet his case is heard. Later reflection contrasts Abel's blood, which cries for vindication, with a better blood that speaks a word of mercy. The plural "bloods" prompted an early Jewish reading that all the descendants who would have come from Abel cry out with him, so that one murder is the destruction of a whole world of lives.

In the ancient Near East, unavenged bloodshed was thought to leave a claim on the community: kin were obliged to seek redress, and blood left uncovered on open ground was a standing accusation until it was answered or ritually covered. Cain has committed the murder in a field, away from witnesses, and disposed of the matter as if secrecy settled it. The scene assumes the world of blood-vengeance but places the role of avenger with God himself rather than with a human kinsman — there is, in the narrative's own terms, no clan left to prosecute the case.

text: Now you are cursed, driven from the ground that opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew says simply "cursed are you from the ground" (min ha'adamah). The preposition min is ambiguous and has been read in at least three ways: separative ("banished away from the ground"), agentive/source ("cursed by the ground" that now testifies against him), or comparative ("cursed more than the ground" was in 3:17). The rendering "cursed, driven from the ground" makes the separative sense explicit, since the following verses describe Cain leaving the soil he tilled and becoming a wanderer; the added word "driven" is interpretive but matches the sentence Cain himself protests in verse 14. The clause "from your hand" is kept literally rather than paraphrased as "at your hands" so that the concrete Hebrew image of hand, blood, and ground stands intact for the ear.

The verb patsah means to open wide, to gape, and is used of a mouth stretched open to swallow (compare the earth opening its mouth in Numbers 16). The ground is personified twice over: it cries out in verse 10 and drinks in verse 11. "Blood" is plural in Hebrew (deme), a plural regularly used for shed blood, bloodguilt, and murder rather than blood as a substance. The chapter is bound together by the repeated word adamah (ground, soil), the same root behind the name Adam — the man made from soil, whose son now pollutes it.

This is the first time in the Bible that a human being is cursed directly. In chapter 3 the curse fell on the serpent and on the ground, and the man was addressed only through the soil; here the curse rests on Cain himself. The verse also assumes that shed blood defiles the land itself and that the land must in some sense answer for it — a theme developed later in the law's insistence that bloodshed pollutes the land and cannot simply be covered over. Cain's punishment is exile from the very ground that received the blood, an anticipation of the pattern of expulsion that runs through the whole narrative.

In an agrarian world, separation from one's soil meant loss of livelihood, kinship protection, and identity, not merely a change of address. Cain the farmer is severed from the one thing that sustained him. Ancient Near Eastern texts likewise reflect the belief that the earth absorbs spilled blood and that unavenged blood brings ruin on the community; the murderer's exile removes the pollution from the land.

Some ancient versions understood the preposition differently, reading the curse as falling "upon the ground" or "on the earth" rather than as a banishment from it, which shows how early the ambiguity was felt. The consonantal Hebrew text itself is stable across the manuscript tradition here.

text: When you work the ground, it will no longer yield its strength to you. You will be a restless wanderer on the earth."

footnotes.text: "It will no longer yield its strength to you" renders a Hebrew idiom literally meaning "it will not continue to give its strength to you." "Strength" (koach) here stands for the soil's productive power — its yield or crop — so some render it "it will no longer give you its produce." The phrase "a restless wanderer" translates two Hebrew participles joined by "and" (na wanad), a doubling that intensifies rather than lists two separate states; alternatives include "a fugitive and a wanderer" or "a ceaseless drifter." The single compact phrase was chosen to preserve the terse, chant-like rhythm of the Hebrew when read aloud. "On the earth" translates ba'arets; the same root ('adamah/'erets) shifts here from the cultivated "ground" of the first line to the wider "earth" over which Cain must roam.

The verse turns on wordplay. Cain, the tiller of 'adamah (ground), is cut off from the 'adamah — the very word that names both his vocation and the humanity ('adam) formed from it. The pair na wanad is an assonant jingle, two short rhyming words that sound like restless motion; nad (to wander, sway) later echoes in the name of the land of Nod, where Cain settles. The verb tosef ("you will not continue/add") stresses cessation of something that was previously happening: the ground had given its strength before, and now stops.

The curse intensifies the judgment of the garden. There the ground was cursed and would yield thorns, yet still yield; here the ground refuses Cain entirely. Bloodshed is portrayed as defiling the land itself, a theme running through the law and the prophets. Interpreters differ on whether the sentence is purely punitive or also protective — the wandering removes Cain from settled society but keeps him alive, and the mark given shortly after makes divine restraint explicit. Cain's response in the next verse shows he hears the sentence as unbearable, raising the question of whether the penalty is retributive justice, mercy short of death, or both.

In an agrarian world, land was identity, security and kinship. To be barred from productive soil and forced into perpetual movement meant loss of clan protection, of ancestral burial ground, and of any legal standing — effectively outlawry. Ancient Near Eastern texts likewise treat exile and homelessness as a punishment ranking just below execution. The irony is sharp: Cain the farmer is condemned to the landless life, while his murdered brother had been a herdsman.

text: Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew noun ʿawon covers the deed ("iniquity"), the state of guilt, and the consequence ("punishment"), and the verb nasaʾ means "lift, carry, bear." So the clause can be heard either as "my punishment is too great to bear" or as "my guilt is too great to be forgiven." The rendering here follows the first path, since Cain's next words (v. 14) complain about the sentence rather than confess the crime. Others render it "My iniquity is greater than can be pardoned," which is equally defensible. Note also that the closing quotation mark is withheld: Cain's speech runs on without a break into v. 14, and for oral reading the two verses are best voiced as one continuous protest.

The construction is comparative min plus the infinitive construct nesoʾ — literally "great is my ʿawon from bearing" — a standard Hebrew way of saying "too great to be borne." Because the infinitive has no expressed subject, the bearer is left open: Cain himself, or God. The idiom nasaʾ ʿawon is used elsewhere both of a guilty party enduring the consequences of sin and of God "lifting away" sin, that is, forgiving it; the same two-sided expression appears in the divine self-description of the LORD as one who bears iniquity. The wording is thus deliberately, or at least unavoidably, double-edged.

Readers have long disputed whether these words are the beginning of repentance or the last gasp of self-concern. Read as "my punishment is too great," Cain protests the sentence and never names his brother; read as "my guilt is too great to be forgiven," he despairs of a mercy that might in fact have been available — a despair that early interpreters treated as a further sin, since God's readiness to pardon exceeds any human crime. Some rabbinic readers took the line as a question flung back at God: "Is my sin too heavy for you to bear?" In every reading, the striking thing is that God answers not with argument but with protection (v. 15).

The early Greek and Latin translations understood the verse in the "forgiveness" direction, rendering it roughly "my guilt is too great for me to be pardoned," and the Aramaic paraphrases move the same way, expanding it into a meditation on whether Cain's sin was greater than God's capacity to forgive. The consonantal Hebrew text itself is stable here; the divergence among ancient versions reflects interpretation of an ambiguous idiom, not differing manuscripts.

text: Look, today you are driving me from the face of the ground, and I will be hidden from your presence. I will be a restless wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."

versions.text: Today you are driving me from the face of the ground, and I will be hidden from your presence. I will be a restless wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."
versions.explanation: The opening particle הֵן ("look/behold") is untranslated. Restoring it preserves the emphatic, pleading tone of Cain's speech and gives the sentence a stronger opening beat for oral reading. The rest of the verse reads naturally and accurately.

footnotes.text: "Look" renders the Hebrew particle *hēn*, a marker of urgent attention that introduces the grounds of a complaint; "behold" is traditional but archaic for reading aloud, and "see" or "here" are also possible. The verse distinguishes two Hebrew words that English often blurs: *ʾădāmâ*, the arable "ground" Cain once tilled (rendered "the face of the ground"), and *ʾereṣ*, the wider "earth" over which he must now roam. Keeping both distinct preserves the contrast between the soil that has rejected him and the open world that receives him. "I will be hidden from your presence" translates a passive-reflexive verb form (*ʾessātēr*) that could equally be rendered actively, "I must hide myself from your face"; the passive was chosen because Cain is describing what the sentence does to him, not a choice he makes. "Restless wanderer" compresses a two-word Hebrew phrase (see the linguistic note); "a fugitive and a wanderer" is a common alternative, but the tighter phrase reads better in a spoken line.

The pair *nāʿ wā-nād*, "tottering and wandering," is a rhyming word-pair built on similar-sounding roots — a sound effect impossible to reproduce exactly in English. It also sets up a play on the place-name Nod (v. 16), the "land of Wandering," where Cain finally settles: the man condemned to have no place ends up in a place named for placelessness. The repeated *pānîm* ("face") is another deliberate echo: Cain is driven from the *face* of the ground and hidden from the *face* of God. In the same idiom, the earlier phrase about sin "crouching at the door" and Cain's fallen "face" (4:5–7) belong to the same web of imagery.

Cain treats banishment from the soil and banishment from God's presence as one and the same loss, reflecting an ancient sense that access to God is bound to place, land, and worship. His words are the first human statement in Scripture about being cut off from God's face — a theme later taken up by the psalmists and prophets. Interpreters differ on whether Cain is repenting or merely protesting: v. 13 can be read either as "my sin is too great to be forgiven" or "my punishment is too great to bear," and this verse, with its focus on personal danger rather than on Abel, has led many readers to hear self-pity rather than contrition. Yet God answers the complaint with protection (v. 15), so that even the archetypal murderer lives under a divine guarantee.

"Whoever finds me will kill me" assumes the ancient practice of blood vengeance, in which the nearest kinsman of a murdered person was obliged to avenge the death. Cain's terror is that, having been expelled from his family's land, he has no clan to shelter him and no settled community to enforce restraint; a landless man was legally and physically defenseless. The question of who these potential killers are has occupied readers since antiquity — the narrative is not concerned to give a population census but to describe the condition of an outcast in a world governed by kinship protection.

The Hebrew opens with a statement, "Look, you have driven me out today," while the early Greek tradition reads it as a condition, "If you drive me out today..." — likely an interpretive smoothing rather than a different Hebrew reading. Some ancient versions also add "and it shall be" or expand the final clause slightly; none of these affects the sense. The verb rendered "you are driving me" is a completed form in Hebrew, expressing a sentence already pronounced and effectively in force, which is why the present tense suits the English.

text: Then the LORD said to him, "Therefore, whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would strike him down.

versions.text: But the LORD said to him, "Not so. Whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance seven times over." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would strike him down.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads לָכֵן, "therefore," which introduces the LORD's protective decree. Rendering it "Not so" reflects an emended reading (לֹא כֵן) attested only in some ancient versions, not the Hebrew text being translated. "Therefore" also flows naturally after Cain's complaint. Additionally, the opening conjunction is a plain narrative connective, so "Then" reads better than the contrastive "But," which was tied to the "Not so" reading.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew is compressed and could be rendered several ways. Literally the clause reads "all/whoever kills Cain, sevenfold it shall be avenged" — an impersonal passive that leaves unstated who exacts the vengeance. "Will suffer vengeance seven times over" keeps the threat impersonal (God stands behind it) while reading smoothly aloud; alternatives include "will be avenged sevenfold" or "vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold." The word rendered "mark" is the ordinary Hebrew word for "sign"; the phrase can equally mean God gave Cain a sign, not necessarily something inscribed on his body. "Put a mark on Cain" follows the most common understanding, but "gave Cain a sign" is fully defensible. The final clause literally reads "so as not to strike him — anyone finding him," deliberately echoing Cain's own words in the previous verse.

Sevenfold (shiv'atayim) is a dual form used adverbially, a stock way of expressing completeness or overwhelming measure rather than an exact count. The verb yuqqam belongs to the root n-q-m, "avenge, take vengeance" — the same root that will resound in Lamech's boast a few verses later. Note the tight verbal linkage: Cain fears "whoever finds me will kill me," and God answers with "whoever kills Cain" and "anyone who finds him," turning Cain's own fearful vocabulary back as a guarantee. The word 'ot, "sign," is used elsewhere of the rainbow, of circumcision, and of the Sabbath — signs that mark a relationship or a pledge, which suggests protection rather than stigma.

The Septuagint and some other early witnesses read the opening word not as lakhen, "therefore," but as lo khen, "not so" — that is, God contradicting Cain: "Not so; whoever kills Cain..." The consonants are nearly identical in Hebrew, and both readings make sense. The Masoretic "therefore" is followed here as the better-attested text.

The mark is grace, not branding: it is given to shield the murderer, not to advertise his guilt. The popular notion of a "mark of Cain" as a curse or a badge of shame reverses the plain sense of the verse, and the text says nothing about what the sign looked like — later speculation about a physical deformity, a tattoo, or skin color has no basis here and has been put to shameful use. Theologically the verse holds two things together: Cain must bear the consequences of his act, yet God restrains further bloodshed and keeps vengeance out of human hands. The sevenfold threat also sets up a deliberate contrast with Lamech, who boasts of seventy-sevenfold revenge — divine restraint answered by human escalation.

In the ancient world, a person cut off from clan and settled land had no legal protection; blood vengeance by a victim's kin was the ordinary mechanism of justice, and a wanderer without kin was fair game. God's declaration functions much like a treaty guarantee or a mark of ownership placed on a protected person, warning off potential avengers. Sevenfold retribution as a formula for disproportionate deterrence appears elsewhere in the ancient Near East and in the Psalms and Proverbs.

text: So Cain went out from the LORD's presence and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "went out from before the face of the LORD." The rendering "from the LORD's presence" keeps the phrase compact and readable aloud, while preserving the sense of departure from a place of encounter and access. Some render it "away from the presence of the LORD" to stress separation; the simpler possessive form was chosen here for rhythm. The opening "So" carries the Hebrew narrative connector (waw), linking Cain's departure to the sentence and the protective mark just given. "Settled" translates a verb that can mean both "sat down" and "dwelt"; the settled sense is chosen because Cain establishes a home and, in the next verse, builds a city. The place name is left untranslated as "Nod" rather than rendered "Wandering," since the text presents it as a proper name; the wordplay is explained in the note below. "East of Eden" follows the most common understanding of the Hebrew phrase, though "in front of Eden" or "opposite Eden" is also defensible.

The name Nod (nod) is built from the same root as the word nad, "wanderer, fugitive," used twice in Cain's sentence and his complaint (vv. 12, 14). Cain is condemned to be a restless wanderer, and the land he lands in is literally "the land of Wandering" — a settled place with an unsettled name, which is the point of the irony. The phrase rendered "east of Eden" uses a construct form of the noun qedem, a word meaning both "east" and "front, what lies before"; the same double sense appears in Hebrew's orientation toward the sunrise, where facing east is facing forward.

To go out "from the LORD's presence" is the sharpest note of the whole episode: exile from God is a deeper loss than exile from the soil. The verse completes a movement begun in chapter 3 — humanity is driven eastward, away from the garden, with each step widening the distance. Yet the departure is not abandonment: Cain leaves under a protective mark, still guarded by the God he leaves. Interpreters differ on whether "the presence" means a localized place of worship near Eden or the relational nearness of God generally; either way, the verse holds together judgment and mercy without resolving the tension.

No land of Nod is known from any ancient geography, inscription, or map, and no serious attempt to locate it has succeeded. The name functions symbolically within the narrative rather than as a real region. Movement eastward is a recurring marker in these early chapters, often signaling drift away from the place of blessing. The immediate move from wandering to city-building in the next verse reflects the ancient world's sense that settled urban life began with a break from an older, freer existence.

text: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and gave birth to Enoch. Cain was building a city, and he named it after his son Enoch.

footnotes.text: "Knew his wife" preserves the Hebrew verb yadaʿ ("to know") exactly as it stands. It is a well-known biblical euphemism for sexual union, and plainer renderings such as "had relations with" or "lay with" are possible; but the literal wording has been kept because it reads with dignity aloud and because the same idiom recurs throughout these chapters (compare 4:1, 4:25). The second half of the verse is compressed in Hebrew: literally "and he was building a city, and he called the name of the city like the name of his son, Enoch." "Cain" has been supplied as the subject of "was building" for clarity in reading aloud, since Hebrew leaves the pronoun unexpressed and a reader could momentarily attach it to Enoch. "He named it after his son Enoch" renders the fuller Hebrew phrase idiomatically rather than word for word.

The clause wayhî bōneh ("he was building") uses a participle with the verb "to be," a construction that expresses ongoing or repeated action rather than a single completed act — the sense is that Cain was engaged in the work of city-building. The name Enoch (Ḥanôk) is related to the root ḥanak, "to dedicate, initiate, train," the same root behind the word for the dedication of a building or altar. There is thus a quiet wordplay: the founder dedicates his city with a name that itself means "dedication." Hebrew ʿîr ("city") covers anything from a walled settlement to a modest fortified enclosure, and need not imply a large urban center.

The identity of Cain's wife is not stated, and the narrative shows no interest in the question. Ancient Jewish tradition generally assumed she was a sister, since Genesis 5:4 notes that Adam fathered sons and daughters; some later writings even supply her with a name. The text's silence suggests the narrator is tracing lines of descent and culture rather than answering questions of population.

City-building in the ancient Near East was a prestigious act, often credited in Mesopotamian tradition to gods, kings, or primeval heroes. Genesis assigns it instead to Cain's line, which in the following verses is also credited with herding, music, and metalworking — the foundations of civilization emerging from the family of the first murderer. Archaeologically, walled settlements in the region are very old, and the note fits a world in which a "city" could be a small fortified cluster of dwellings.

There is a pointed irony here: the man sentenced to be a restless wanderer (4:12) settles down and builds a walled city, seeking by his own effort the security God had already promised him by a mark of protection. Interpreters have read this in two directions. Some see defiance — human self-protection substituted for divine keeping, the city as a monument to a name Cain wants remembered. Others see God's common grace, allowing culture, craft, and community to flourish even in a cursed line. The naming of the city after his son also raises the theme of legacy: Cain builds and names, while it is Seth's line that will "call on the name of the LORD" (4:26).

The verse is stable across the manuscript tradition; the ancient versions all agree with the received Hebrew text, differing only in the transliteration of the name Enoch. Some early interpreters, troubled by the sequence, took Enoch rather than Cain as the builder — an alternative supported by no textual variant, only by reading the unexpressed subject differently.

text: To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael, and Mehujael was the father of Methushael, and Methushael was the father of Lamech.

footnotes.text: The verse opens with a passive verb form, literally "and there was born to Enoch Irad," which the translation preserves as "To Enoch was born Irad." The remaining links use the active verb "begot/fathered," rendered here as "was the father of" for smoother oral delivery; the older "begat" carries the same sense but is archaic when read aloud. The repeated pattern of name-plus-verb is kept intentionally, since the chain-like repetition is the point of a genealogy and gives the sentence its rhythm when spoken.

The verb ילד (yalad) means "to bear, bring forth"; in the passive stem it describes the child being born, in the causative/active stem the parent's role in producing offspring. Hebrew uses the same root for both mother and father, so "fathered" is an interpretive narrowing that the context requires. The names themselves are compact sentences or descriptions: Mehujael and Methushael both end in -el, "God," and Methushael likely echoes an old Semitic form meaning "man of God"; Mehujael has been read either as "struck by God" or "God gives life," and Irad's meaning remains uncertain, possibly connected to a word for "wild donkey" or to a city name.

Within this single verse the same person's name is written two different ways in the Hebrew consonantal text: first Mehuyael, then Mehiyyael. Ancient versions and some manuscripts smooth this out to one spelling, and the translation likewise uses a single form so the listener is not confused into hearing two people. Some witnesses also read the opening verb as active, "Enoch fathered Irad," matching the pattern of the rest of the verse rather than the passive of the received Hebrew text.

Genealogies functioned in the ancient world as charters of identity, tracing craft, land and clan rather than merely satisfying curiosity about ancestry. This seven-generation line from Adam through Cain to Lamech's sons is structured to reach a climax in the following verses, where the origins of herding, music and metalwork are traced to Lamech's children. Names of this type, several with Mesopotamian resonance, suggest the list preserves very old traditional material.

The names in Cain's line closely resemble those in Seth's line in the next chapter: Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methushael and Lamech stand alongside Enoch, Jared, Mahalalel, Methuselah and Lamech. Interpreters differ on whether these are two versions of one tradition or two deliberately paired lines meant to be compared — the one culminating in Lamech's song of vengeance, the other in Enoch who walked with God and in Noah. Read as a pair, they set two trajectories of human history side by side without yet pronouncing judgment on either.

text: Lamech took two wives for himself; one was named Adah, and the other Zillah.

versions.text: Lamech took two wives; one was named Adah and the other Zillah.
versions.explanation: Restores the reflexive sense of Hebrew לוֹ ("for himself"), which subtly marks Lamech's self-willed action, and adds a comma before "and the other" to give the reader a natural breathing point in oral reading.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads more fully, "And Lamech took for himself two wives; the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the second was Zillah." For oral flow the doubled naming formula has been shortened to "one was named Adah, and the other Zillah," letting the verb carry over into the second clause rather than repeating "the name of." The phrase "for himself" renders the Hebrew dative of advantage and has been kept because it subtly stresses Lamech's own initiative and self-interest; some renderings drop it as redundant. "Took two wives" preserves the plain Hebrew idiom for marrying rather than smoothing it to "married two women," since the verb "take" is the standard marriage term throughout these narratives. Hebrew literally says "the second," but idiomatic English prefers "the other" when only two are in view.

The verb לָקַח (laqach, "take") with "a woman/wife" as object is the ordinary Hebrew expression for entering marriage; it carries no implication of seizure by itself. Both names may be significant: Adah (עָדָה) is commonly linked to the root for "adornment, ornament" (compare עֲדִי), while Zillah (צִלָּה) is usually connected with צֵל, "shade, shadow," perhaps suggesting protection or shelter. Hebrew marks the two women with "the one" (feminine הָאַחַת) and "the second" (הַשֵּׁנִית), a counting pattern used elsewhere for pairs.

This is the first explicit mention of a man with two wives in the biblical narrative. In the ancient Near East polygamy was legally recognized and often tied to status, wealth, and the desire for numerous offspring; marriage was normally arranged with a bride payment and family negotiation, which makes the active "took for himself" language typical of such accounts. Lamech's household is described in terms of prestige and power, and the following verses attach the origins of herding, music, and metalworking to his sons.

Interpreters have long noted that the notice of two wives stands in tension with the pattern of one man and one woman becoming "one flesh" described earlier, and that it appears within the line of Cain, immediately before Lamech's boast about vengeance. Many read the placement as part of a narrative portrait of escalating human self-assertion rather than as approval. The text itself reports the arrangement without comment, and Scripture elsewhere records polygamy among figures it treats sympathetically, so the moral judgment here is conveyed by context and literary placement rather than by direct condemnation.

text: Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads compactly, "the father of one dwelling in a tent and livestock," joining a single participle ("dwelling") to two objects that do not fit it equally well — one can dwell in a tent but not in livestock. The translation supplies a second verb, "keep livestock," to make the sense plain in English, and renders the singular participle as a plural ("those who live") since it stands for a whole class of people, matching the parallel phrasing in the next verse. "Father" is kept literal rather than rendered "ancestor" or "founder," preserving the ring of the Hebrew idiom while the following words make its meaning clear.

The spelling "Jabal" follows the Hebrew Yabal; the form "Jabel" also appears in older usage. The vowel pattern deliberately echoes his brother Yubal (Jubal) in verse 21 and Tubal-Cain in verse 22 — three names built on a similar sound.

The name Yabal is often linked to the root ybl, "to lead, bring, carry along" (used of flowing streams and of leading animals), which suits a driver of herds; some connect it to a word for a stream or watercourse. Yubal in the next verse resembles yobel, the ram's horn or trumpet, fitting a musician. The Hebrew word 'av, "father," is regularly used for the originator or archetype of a trade, way of life, or people, not only for a biological parent. Miqneh, "livestock," is derived from the verb "to acquire" — cattle as movable property and wealth.

Ancient translators noticed the awkward pairing and smoothed it out: some rendered the phrase as "father of those living in tents, herdsmen of cattle," supplying the missing verbal idea just as modern versions do. The consonantal Hebrew text itself is stable in the manuscript tradition; the variation lies in how the versions handle the compressed syntax.

Tent-dwelling with flocks and herds describes the semi-nomadic pastoralism widespread across the ancient Near East, a way of life later shared by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The verses about Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-Cain form a short catalogue of culture-founders — herding, music, metalwork — a type of tradition known from other ancient accounts that trace the crafts of civilization back to named ancestors.

These achievements are credited to the line of Cain, and interpreters have read that in different ways. Some see a sober acknowledgment that human culture and skill are genuine gifts, arising even in a family marked by violence. Others stress the placement beside Lamech's boast of vengeance in the following verses, reading the passage as showing civilization advancing while sin advances with it. Either way, the text presents the arts of herding, music, and metal as human developments rather than divine revelations.

text: His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all who play the lyre and the pipe.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally reads "the father of all who grasp (or handle) the lyre and the pipe"; the verb tafas means to seize or take hold of, and is the standard idiom for taking up and playing an instrument, so "play" renders the sense naturally. "Father" is kept literal, matching verse 20, since it functions here as the title of a founder or originator of a craft rather than a biological ancestor. Kinnor is a stringed instrument of the lyre family, rendered "harp" in older tradition; ugav is a wind instrument, rendered variously "pipe," "flute," or (in an older rendering that misled many readers) "organ." Together they stand for the two great families of instruments, strings and winds, and thus for music as a whole. The two short clauses are kept as two beats separated by a semicolon, echoing the rhythm of the previous verse so the pair of brothers is heard as a pair.

The three brothers' names chime together: Jabal, Jubal, Tubal — all built on sounds connected with the root y-b-l, "to bring, lead, carry along." Jubal in particular echoes yobel, the ram's horn blown at festivals and in the Jubilee year, so the musician's very name sounds like a trumpet blast. Kinnor is an ancient word shared across Semitic languages and even borrowed into Egyptian and Greek; ugav appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible and its precise identification remains uncertain, though its pairing with a stringed instrument marks it as a wind instrument.

Lyres and pipes are among the oldest instruments known from the ancient Near East. Lyres appear on Sumerian remains from the third millennium BC, in Egyptian tomb paintings, and on wall reliefs and seals across Canaan; reed and bone pipes have been recovered from excavations throughout the region. The kinnor was a portable, hand-held lyre, played by shepherds and court musicians alike, and pipes accompanied both feasting and mourning. The verse thus places the origins of music alongside herding and metalworking as one of the founding trades of settled human life.

It is striking that the arts of civilization — herding, music, metalwork — are traced through the line of Cain, the first murderer. Interpreters have read this in opposing ways. Some see a warning: human culture flourishes even as it grows apart from God, and the same line produces Lamech's boast of vengeance a few verses later. Others read it more generously, as testimony that the creative gifts of God are not withdrawn from fallen humanity, and that music, craft and skill remain genuine goods however tangled their origins. The text itself offers no judgment, simply recording that this is how music came into the world.

The Greek tradition renders the two instruments as psaltery and lyre, and the Latin as cithara and organum — the latter being the source of the older English "organ," which suggests a far later instrument than anything the Hebrew has in view. The consonantal Hebrew text is stable here, with no significant variants.

text: Zillah also gave birth to Tubal-Cain, who forged all kinds of tools out of bronze and iron. Tubal-Cain's sister was Naamah.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew of the middle clause is compressed and difficult: literally "a sharpener/hammerer of every cutter (or engraver) of bronze and iron." The participle *lotesh* means to hammer or whet metal, and *choresh* denotes one who cuts, engraves, or fashions — but the two participles stacked together are awkward, and the object of the sharpening is unstated. The rendering "who forged all kinds of tools out of bronze and iron" takes the phrase as a description of Tubal-Cain's craft and supplies "tools" for the sake of clear oral reading. Other defensible renderings are "who sharpened every implement of bronze and iron" or, following the pattern of verses 20–21, "the father of all who work bronze and iron." The final clause is a bare noun sentence, "and the sister of Tubal-Cain, Naamah"; the added verb "was" makes it a complete English sentence. "Also" renders *gam-hi*, "she too," which ties Zillah's offspring back to Adah's in verses 20–21.

The name Tubal-Cain joins Tubal with Cain (*qayin*), a word that in related Semitic languages (Aramaic and Arabic *qayn*) means "smith" or "metalworker" — a fitting play for the ancestor of metallurgy, and an echo of the Cain from whom this line descends. Naamah comes from the root *n-ʿ-m*, "to be pleasant, lovely," so her name means something like "Lovely" or "Pleasant One." The construction *gam-hi* ("she too") is emphatic, pairing Zillah with Adah.

The clause about Tubal-Cain's craft is unusually terse, and ancient translators handled it in different ways: Greek tradition simplifies to something like "he was a hammerer, a smith in bronze and iron," while other early versions render him "a master of every craftsman in bronze and iron." Some scholars propose that the word "father" (*avi*), which appears in the parallel notices of verses 20 and 21, once stood here as well and dropped out in copying; the Hebrew as preserved has no such word, and this translation follows the received text.

Metalworking was among the most prized and closely guarded skills of the ancient world, and smiths often formed distinct guilds or clans; the Kenites, whose name shares the root of Cain, were later associated with such itinerant metal trades. The name Tubal also designates a region in eastern Anatolia (Assyrian Tabal) long famous for its copper and iron production, which may lie behind the association. Bronze — copper alloyed with tin — was the dominant working metal for centuries before iron came into widespread use, and naming both together marks Tubal-Cain as the originator of the whole metal-working tradition rather than of one period's technology.

This genealogy credits the line of Cain with the foundations of civilized life — herding, music, and metalwork — a striking acknowledgment that human culture is a genuine good even when it arises from a family under a curse. Yet the placement is pointed: the mention of forged bronze and iron leads straight into Lamech's boast of vengeance in the next verse, suggesting that the tools of craft and the weapons of violence come from the same hand. Naamah is one of few women named in these early genealogies, and later Jewish tradition speculated variously about her identity, in some accounts making her the wife of Noah.

text:
Lamech said to his wives:
"Adah and Zillah, hear my voice;
wives of Lamech, listen to my words.
I have killed a man for wounding me,
a young man for striking me.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb הָרַגְתִּי is a simple perfect, most naturally rendered "I have killed," and that is the reading adopted here. Some understand it as a boast about a future or hypothetical act ("I would kill"), or as a general principle ("I kill"), since Hebrew perfects can express settled resolve. The rendering "a young man" for יֶלֶד keeps the poetic parallel with "a man" while avoiding the impression of a small child; the word covers a boy or a youth. The two Hebrew nouns for injury, פֶּצַע (an open gash) and חֲבוּרָה (a bruise or welt), are given as "wounding me" and "striking me" so that the line reads smoothly aloud; a more literal rendering would be "for my wound... for my bruise." The prefixed preposition לְ is taken causally ("because of"/"in return for"), which suits the boast; it could conceivably be read as result ("so that I was wounded"), but that fits the context of triumph less well. The wives are addressed with feminine plural imperatives, so the commands are directed to them specifically; the closing quotation mark falls at the end of the following verse, since the poem continues.

These lines are a compact piece of Hebrew verse, arranged in the classic pattern of paired half-lines: "Adah and Zillah" matches "wives of Lamech," "hear my voice" matches "listen to my words," and "a man" matches "a young man." The imperatives שְׁמַעַן and הַאְזֵנָּה are archaic feminine plural forms, an old-fashioned flourish that marks the speech as poetry rather than ordinary narration. The verb הַאְזֵנָּה is built from the noun for "ear," so it means literally "give ear." There is also a sound-play across the second half: פִּצְעִי and חַבֻּרָתִי both end with the same possessive suffix, hammering out the rhythm of the boast.

Lamech's song is widely regarded as one of the oldest poetic fragments preserved in the Bible, sometimes called the Song of the Sword. It stands at the end of the Cain genealogy, immediately after the note that Lamech's son forged tools of bronze and iron — the reader is meant to hear the new weaponry behind the new boast. In the honor-based societies of the ancient Near East, blood vengeance was a family duty, but customary law and later legal collections aimed to keep retaliation proportionate to the injury. Lamech's claim to kill a man for a mere bruise is a deliberate rejection of proportion, and it is proclaimed as a matter of pride rather than confessed as guilt.

The verse shows how far violence has spread since Cain: Cain killed and then feared retaliation, while his descendant kills and then sings about it. Where God had limited vengeance against Cain, Lamech seizes vengeance for himself and multiplies it. Read alongside the line about forgiveness "seventy-seven times" in the Gospels, Lamech's arithmetic of revenge becomes the dark mirror of the arithmetic of mercy. Many interpreters see here the narrative purpose of the whole passage: the growth of human culture — cities, herding, music, metalwork — runs side by side with the growth of human violence, so that the flood narrative that follows comes as no surprise.

text:
If Cain is avenged seven times over,
then Lamech seventy-seven times over."

versions.text:
If Cain is avenged seven times over,
then Lamech seventy-seven times."
versions.explanation: The two halves of this poetic line are deliberately parallel in Hebrew (שִׁבְעָתַיִם / שִׁבְעִים וְשִׁבְעָה). Matching the wording exactly ("seven times over" / "seventy-seven times over") strengthens the parallel rhythm for oral reading; as it stands the shift from "times over" to "times" slightly weakens the echo. The conditional rendering of כִּי and the closing quotation mark are otherwise well handled."""

footnotes.text: The opening Hebrew particle ki can mean either "for/because" or "if"; here it introduces the comparison that completes Lamech's boast, so it is rendered "If." The second line has no verb in Hebrew — literally "and Lamech seventy and seven" — so "then... times over" is supplied to carry the sense of the ellipsis and to keep the two lines balanced for reading aloud. The Hebrew verb is passive ("is avenged" / "vengeance is taken for him"), deliberately leaving the avenger unnamed; some render it actively, "whoever kills Cain will suffer vengeance sevenfold." The phrase "seven times over" was preferred to "sevenfold" for its rhythm alongside "seventy-seven times over."

Shiv'atayim is a dual form of "seven" used adverbially, "sevenfold, seven times over." The following phrase is simply "seventy and seven," the ordinary way of counting in Hebrew; it is not a multiplication ("seventy times seven"), though ancient Greek renderings preserved an ambiguity that allowed that reading. The verse is the closing line of a compact poem (vv. 23–24) marked by parallel pairs and intensification: man/young man, wound/bruise, seven/seventy-seven. The root naqam covers avenging, requital, and the settling of blood-debt.
