Lamech's words echo and outbid the divine word over Cain in v. 15, where the Lord decreed a sevenfold requital on anyone who killed him. What was God's protective limit Lamech seizes as his own license, multiplying it more than tenfold: humanity's violence escalates faster than its skill in bronze and iron celebrated in the preceding verses. Many read this "Song of the Sword" as the moral low point of the line of Cain, setting up the contrast with the line of Seth that begins in the next verse. Later Gospel teaching answers the boast directly, replacing "seventy-seven" acts of vengeance with "seventy-seven" acts of forgiveness.

In tribal societies of the ancient Near East, blood vengeance by the wronged family was the ordinary mechanism of justice, and proportionality — a life for a life, a wound for a wound — was the restraint that kept feuds from consuming clans. Lamech's boast breaks that restraint: he kills for a mere wound and threatens disproportionate retaliation against anyone who touches him. Boasting poems recited before wives or a gathered clan are known from the region, and the mention of weapons follows naturally on Tubal-cain's metalworking.

text: Adam knew his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, for she said, "God has granted me another child in place of Abel, since Cain killed him."

footnotes.text: "Knew his wife" preserves the Hebrew verb yada' ("to know"), the same discreet expression used in 4:1; rendering it "lay with" or "made love to" would be clearer but would break the deliberate echo with the opening of the chapter. The word translated "child" is literally "seed" (zera'), a collective term for offspring; "another child" reads more naturally aloud than "another seed" and keeps the focus on the single son just born, though the Hebrew also carries the wider sense of continuing a line of descendants. The word "saying" has been supplied: Hebrew simply joins the naming to the explanation with ki ("for/because"), a standard formula in birth narratives that English needs a speech marker to carry. "Granted" renders shat, literally "set, placed, appointed"; "appointed" would sound the wordplay with the name Seth more strongly but reads stiffly in speech.

The name Shet (Seth) plays on the verb shat, "he set/placed/appointed" — a sound-echo naming of the kind found throughout Genesis, where a name is explained by a similar-sounding word rather than by strict etymology. No English rendering can hold both the sense and the sound; "God has set for me" would keep the assonance faintly but loses the warmth of "granted." Note also that "Adam" appears here without the definite article, functioning as a personal name rather than "the man" as in earlier chapters. The phrase tachat Hevel, "in place of Abel," uses a preposition of substitution and replacement.

Eve speaks of "God" (Elohim) here, whereas in 4:1 at Cain's birth she named the LORD (YHWH); the shift is subtle but has long been noticed by interpreters. The verse marks a turning point: after Cain's murder and Lamech's boast of unlimited vengeance, the narrative resets through a third son. Seth becomes the line through which Genesis 5 traces humanity, and the New Testament genealogy of Jesus runs through Seth rather than Cain. Eve's words attribute the new birth wholly to divine gift, not to human effort — a quiet answer to the violence of the preceding verses.

In the Hebrew Bible mothers frequently name their children and supply the explanation for the name, as Eve does here. Such naming speeches often mark a moment of interpretation, in which the mother reads God's hand in her circumstances. Loss of a son and the hope of a replacement heir was a matter of survival in ancient family life, where descendants secured a household's name, land, and memory.

The Hebrew text has "she called his name Seth," with a feminine verb, making Eve the one who names the child; some ancient witnesses read a masculine form, "he called," attributing the naming to Adam. The feminine reading is well supported and fits the first-person speech that follows ("God has granted me"), and is followed here.

versions.text: Adam knew his wife again, and she gave birth to a son and named him Seth, saying, "God has granted me another child in place of Abel, since Cain killed him."
versions.explanation: The single long sentence stacks three coordinated clauses before the speech marker, which is hard to sustain in one breath when read aloud. "for she said" also renders the Hebrew ki more transparently than the bare participle "saying," while keeping the supplied speech marker noted in the footnote.

text: Seth also had a son, and he named him Enosh. At that time people began to call on the name of the LORD.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with an impersonal passive: "And to Seth also, to him, a son was born." Rendering this as "Seth also had a son" keeps the natural English rhythm while preserving the emphasis of "also" — Seth, like his father, fathers a son and continues the line. In the second clause, "he named him" follows the vocalization that makes Seth the subject; the consonants can also be read as a passive, "his name was called Enosh," which some render "and he was named Enosh." The final clause translates another impersonal passive, literally "then it was begun to call on the name of the LORD"; since Hebrew leaves the actor unnamed, English supplies "people." Alternative renderings include "then men began to invoke the name of the LORD" or "at that time the name of the LORD began to be invoked." As throughout, "the LORD" in capitals represents the personal divine name YHWH.

The name Enosh (אֱנוֹשׁ) is itself an ordinary Hebrew word for "man, human being," often used in poetry with overtones of frailty and mortality (as in "what is man, that you are mindful of him"). So Seth's son bears, in effect, a second version of the name Adam — "humankind" — underscoring that this is the line through which humanity continues. The verb הוּחַל is a passive form of the root ח־ל־ל; when read as "begin," it yields "it was begun." The same consonants belong to a homonymous root meaning "to profane," which opened the door to a very different ancient reading (see the theological note). "To call on the name of" (קָרָא בְּשֵׁם) is a set idiom for invoking a deity in worship, prayer, or public proclamation — not merely uttering a name.

Taken at face value, the verse marks the beginning of organized public worship: after the violence of Cain's line, humanity through Seth begins to invoke God by name. Because the divine name YHWH appears here, some readers see tension with the later statement that the patriarchs did not know God by that name; a common resolution is that the narrator uses the name known to his own audience, or that the later text speaks of knowing the name's full significance rather than its mere use. An ancient Jewish interpretive tradition, exploiting the double meaning of the root, read the line negatively: "then the name of the LORD began to be profaned," locating the origin of idolatry in this generation. Early Christian readers, following a Greek rendering, heard instead a note of hope — humanity's expectant turning toward God.

Some ancient witnesses read the verb differently. A Greek tradition renders it "he hoped to call on the name of the Lord," apparently deriving the form from the root meaning "to wait, hope" rather than "to begin," and makes Enosh the subject. An Aramaic interpretive tradition moves in the opposite direction, reading "then they ceased to pray in the name of the LORD." The Latin tradition agrees with the Hebrew in sense: "he began to call upon the name of the Lord." The consonantal Hebrew text is stable; the differences arise from vocalization and interpretation. The Hebrew text also closes here with a paragraph marker, signaling the end of the section on Cain's and Seth's lines before the genealogy that follows.

Naming a child in the ancient Near East was an act of claiming and interpreting: the name announced hope, circumstance, or destiny. Invoking a deity "by name" presupposes a world of many named gods, in which addressing one specific deity by his own name was the essence of a cult. The verse thus functions as a cultural origin story, noting when human beings first began the practice of formal worship — a common feature of ancient genealogies, which record the beginnings of crafts, cities, and religious customs alongside the births of sons.
